gotchas.gotcha: Commands are NOT protected by unified-creator-guard.cjs (unlike skills, agents, hooks, templates)
gotchas.why_it_happens: Commands are passive markdown prompts with no privilege escalation or integration coupling. Security threat model is equivalent to direct user input. Creator guard overhead not justified.
gotchas.trigger: Developers may expect commands to require skill-creator workflow
gotchas.solution: Commands are user-controlled, lightweight artifacts. Direct writes to .claude/commands/ are intentional and safe. No creator workflow required.
gotchas.alternatives_considered: Protect commands with creator-guard (rejected - adds complexity without proportional security benefit)
gotchas.extracted_from: Task #86 security compliance check, confirmed by Task #83 architecture design

gotchas.gotcha: While thin delegators (3-line shims) are scalable, they can become boilerplate at scale
gotchas.context: Commands System now has 16 identical 3-line delegators (only skill name varies)
gotchas.why_it_happens: Pattern is so simple that adding 1 command requires copy-paste of 3 lines
gotchas.trigger: After 10+ similar delegators are created manually, developers may want to automate
gotchas.solution: For future command additions: consider creating a command generator script or template expansion tool. But don't overcomplicate - 3-line pattern is maintainable
gotchas.future_enhancement: Optional: command-generator.cjs that takes skill name and generates command file

gotchas.gotcha: Enriched commands (/learn that integrates multiple features) can become maintenance burden if overused
gotchas.context: Only /learn enriches beyond single-skill delegation (combines context-compressor + memory protocol)
gotchas.why_it_happens: Developers may want to add convenience commands that combine multiple skills
gotchas.solution: Keep enriched commands rare. Document each enriched command's integration strategy in the catalog. Prefer orchestrating workflows via agent-level task chaining over command-level combinations.
gotchas.pattern: Enriched = single command + documentation of integration. Multi-step = agent delegation.
gotchas.extracted_from: Task #85 catalog design (1 enriched command documented as exception)

gotchas.gotcha: When moving files deeper in directory tree, __dirname-based path calculations must be updated
gotchas.context: Tools System Overhaul Phase C (Task #95) - relocated 8 modules from tools/ to lib/subdirs/
gotchas.why_it_happens: Code computes PROJECT_ROOT using relative paths like resolve(__dirname, '../..'). When file moves from depth 2 (tools/) to depth 3 (lib/workflow/), the depth changes.
gotchas.symptoms: Silent failures when computing PROJECT_ROOT - file operations target wrong directory, config files not found, MODULE_NOT_FOUND for sibling modules
gotchas.trigger: Relocating files from shallow to deep directory (or vice versa) without updating __dirname calculations
gotchas.detection_pattern: Search relocated files for __dirname, verify '../..' count matches new depth
gotchas.solution: Update all __dirname-based paths: resolve(__dirname, '../..') → resolve(__dirname, '../../..'). Better: use helper function that walks up to find .claude/CLAUDE.md
gotchas.example: Moved decision-handler.mjs from tools/workflow/ (depth 2) to lib/workflow/ (depth 3). Required updating resolve(__dirname, '../..') to resolve(__dirname, '../../..')
gotchas.prevention: Create computeProjectRoot() helper that walks directory tree instead of hardcoding depth
gotchas.extracted_from: Task #95 learnings.md, documented in ADR-089 implementation notes

gotchas.gotcha: Security scanner triggers false positives on test files containing intentional malicious strings
gotchas.context: Tools System Overhaul Phase C (Task #95) - decision-handler-security.test.cjs contains malicious expressions for testing
gotchas.why_it_happens: security-lint.cjs scans ALL .js/.cjs/.mjs files for dangerous patterns (eval, new Function, exec). Test files that verify these patterns are rejected correctly contain the patterns themselves.
gotchas.symptoms: security-lint.cjs fails on test files with ERROR: 'eval detected' or 'new Function detected' even though usage is safe (inside test strings)
gotchas.trigger: Creating security tests that include malicious code samples as test data
gotchas.solution: Add '// security-lint-ignore: Security test file - contains intentional malicious strings for validation' as first line of test file. Scanner skips files with this directive.
gotchas.example: decision-handler-security.test.cjs has malicious expression strings like 'process.exit(1)' and 'require("fs")' for testing parser rejection
alternatives: Extend security-lint.cjs to auto-detect test files (path includes tests/ or *.test.*)
Store malicious test data in separate .json file outside scan scope
Configure security-lint.cjs to allow eval/Function in test files only
gotchas.best_practice: Always include reason in ignore directive: // security-lint-ignore: <clear explanation>

gotchas.gotcha: Consumer discovery grep patterns may miss dynamic require statements and template-string imports in relocated modules
gotchas.context: Scripts System Overhaul Pipeline #8 (Task #99) - 2 scripts missed in Phase C (Task #95) consumer discovery despite comprehensive grep
gotchas.why_it_happens: Phase C (Task #95) used grep for static `require('literal-path')` patterns. However, dynamic requires like `require('.' + moduleName)` or template strings like ``require(`path/${dir}`)`` bypass literal pattern matching. Additionally, grep may miss requires in script files if search scope doesn't include scripts/ directory.
gotchas.symptoms: Scripts fail with MODULE_NOT_FOUND at runtime despite comprehensive grep-based consumer discovery. Example: validate-index.mjs phantom import was missed, breaking validate:full CI chain.
gotchas.trigger: Relocating a file from one directory to another (git mv) without exhaustive consumer discovery. Phase C coverage was 45+ imports, but 2 scripts (validate-index.mjs, validate-all-references.mjs) in scripts/ directory were missed.
gotchas.solution: Enhance consumer discovery to (1) include scripts/ directory explicitly, (2) use broader regex patterns that catch dynamic requires and template strings, (3) test by running affected npm scripts after relocation to catch runtime failures early
gotchas.example: validate-index.mjs has import statement: `import { contextPathResolver } from '../../.claude/tools/context/context-path-resolver.mjs'` (old path after Phase C relocation) → ERROR: MODULE_NOT_FOUND
prevention: grep for filename alone: `grep -r 'context-path-resolver' .` (not just path patterns)
grep for old directory path: `grep -r 'tools/context' .` (catches any reference)
Test npm scripts: `pnpm validate:full` would have failed immediately, revealing the phantom import
Run full test suite before committing relocations
gotchas.best_practice: After any file relocation: (1) grep filename, (2) grep old directory path, (3) run all affected npm scripts, (4) run full test suite
gotchas.extracted_from: Task #99 learnings (Script Import Regression Prevention), Task #95 post-QA fixes (Task #97)

gotchas.gotcha: Architecture plan documents may be referenced in ADRs but not actually created, creating false expectations
gotchas.context: Scripts System Overhaul Pipeline #8 (ADR-090) references `.claude/context/plans/scripts-overhaul-architecture-2026-02-07.md` that does not exist
gotchas.why_it_happens: During ADR authoring, the architecture plan is referenced as a separate document (following the pattern from other ADRs like ADR-087, ADR-089). However, the actual document file is not created. All work is completed correctly per the ADR, but the plan document itself is missing.
gotchas.symptoms: Reference to architecture plan fails when trying to link or read the document. Example: 'Architecture Plan: `.claude/context/plans/scripts-overhaul-architecture-2026-02-07.md`' but file is not found.
gotchas.trigger: Creating comprehensive ADRs without ensuring all referenced artifacts (plans, documents, reports) are actually created
gotchas.solution: After creating an ADR that references a plan document, verify the document exists. If it doesn't, either (1) create it by extracting relevant sections from the ADR, (2) remove the reference and note that implementation followed the ADR directly, or (3) mark it as TODO for future extraction.
prevention: Checklist in ADR authoring: verify all artifact references exist
Use relative path references in ADRs only if documents are guaranteed to exist
Consider creating plan documents programmatically from ADR sections
gotchas.impact: Minor - all work was completed correctly per ADR; plan document is not critical to understanding what was done, but reduces completeness
gotchas.extracted_from: Task #101 finalization review, noted during reflection evaluation

gotchas.gotcha: Adding compatibility documentation without creating full cross-platform equivalent leaves the problem partially solved
gotchas.context: Scripts System Overhaul Pipeline #8 (Task #100) addressed validate-sync.sh Windows incompatibility by adding comments, but did not create full Node.js equivalent
gotchas.why_it_happens: When a tool has platform-specific limitations (bash-only on Windows), developers often add documentation explaining the limitation and providing workarounds. While this is an improvement, it's not a full solution. Users still cannot run the tool natively on Windows without workarounds.
gotchas.symptoms: Windows users must use WSL, Git Bash, or Cygwin to run validate-sync.sh. The documentation explains this, but users still cannot use the tool directly.
gotchas.trigger: Time constraints or complexity of creating cross-platform equivalent. Bash scripts that use Unix tools (find, grep, sed, etc.) are complex to port to Node.js.
gotchas.solution: For high-value scripts (critical in CI/CD), create a Node.js equivalent that provides identical functionality cross-platform. For lower-priority scripts, documentation + workarounds may be sufficient.
gotchas.example: validate-sync.sh uses `find`, `grep`, `xargs` to validate file synchronization. Creating Node.js equivalent (validate-sync.mjs) would enable Windows users to run it natively.
gotchas.assessment: validate-sync.sh is not critical (alternative validation scripts exist: validate:config, validate:references, validate:full). Documentation + workarounds are sufficient. Future enhancement: create Node.js equivalent if Windows compatibility becomes high-priority.
gotchas.extracted_from: Task #100 learnings (GAP-6 Windows compatibility), reflection analysis

gotchas.gotcha: Thin rules (3-7 lines) are worse than no rules -- they consume system prompt tokens without providing actionable guidance
gotchas.context: Rules System Overhaul Pipeline #9 (Task #102-103) found 7 of 9 rule files were only 3-8 lines each, providing minimal guidance
gotchas.why_it_happens: Rules are auto-loaded into system prompt (every line costs tokens). When a rule provides only generic platitudes (e.g., 'Prefer composition over inheritance', 'Avoid console logging'), it adds noise without signal. The developer already knows this. The rule's value is project-specific guidance, not generic best practices.
gotchas.symptoms: Rule file exists but is too thin to be useful. Developers read it once and forget. It consumes ~50 tokens per rule without changing behavior. At 9 rules × 50 tokens = 450 tokens of baseline cost for thin rules.
gotchas.trigger: Creating a rule file with less than 6 directives. Initial impulse: 'A short rule is better than no rule.' Actual result: 'A short generic rule is noise.'
gotchas.solution: Minimum 6+ actionable directives per rule, with project-specific context. Examples: Instead of 'Favor immutability', write 'Avoid in-place mutation of objects; use spread operator or Object.assign() for shallow copies, and libraries like immer for nested updates.'
gotchas.example_before: coding-style.md (8 lines): 5 bullet points, all generic, no project context
gotchas.example_after: code-standards.md (44 lines): 8 sections with 40+ directives, all with project-specific context (file extensions, test structure, .cjs vs .mjs conventions)
gotchas.expansion_impact: Pipeline #9 expanded 7 thin rules from 3-8 lines to 33-54 lines each. Token cost increased from ~350 to ~3500 tokens (+7x), but coverage improved (added memory protocol, task tracking rules that filled critical gaps). ROI: +7x tokens for +3 new rules and 2 filled behavioral gaps.
gotchas.pattern: After creating a rule, check: 'Does this rule provide project-specific guidance that would change a developer's behavior?' If not, expand or delete.
gotchas.extracted_from: Task #102-103 rules audit and expansion, learnings.md entry on thin rule analysis

gotchas.gotcha: After merging files (e.g., coding-style.md + patterns.md into code-standards.md), references to the deleted filenames can break in other documentation files
gotchas.context: Rules System Overhaul Pipeline #9 (Task #103-104) merged coding-style.md and patterns.md into code-standards.md. Later discovered 5 broken references to the deleted files.
gotchas.why_it_happens: When merging files, developers update obvious references (imports, includes, links in README), but miss references in comment tables, historical notes, architecture docs, and examples. References in `.claude/` subdirectories are easy to miss because they're not in the main codebase.
gotchas.symptoms: Old filenames still mentioned in documentation: '@DIRECTORY_STRUCTURE.md (rule listing table)', 'templates/README.md (deleted files)', 'templates/_archive/README.md (archive tracking)', 'rules-system-security-review.md (enforcement table)', 'CLAUDE.md (Section 7)'. These create confusion: 'Is coding-style.md still a rule?' Users may search for the old file and get 404.
gotchas.trigger: Merging two files without doing exhaustive grep search for all references. Initial approach: grep for 'coding-style' and 'patterns' with limited scope. Actual references exist in: directory listings, archive notes, security docs, enforcement tables, cross-references.
gotchas.solution: After ANY file deletion/merge/rename: 1) `grep -r 'old-filename' .claude/` across entire framework directory (not just code), 2) Search for old filename in ALL `.md` files (architecture docs, catalogs, plans, reports), 3) Update all references. Pattern: file deletions require broader search scope than developers expect.
example_broken_references: @DIRECTORY_STRUCTURE.md: 'Section 9.1 lists rules: agents.md, coding-style.md, patterns.md...' (should be: ...code-standards.md...)
templates/README.md: 'Deleted rules: coding-style.md and patterns.md' (implies they're archived, but they're merged into code-standards.md)
templates/_archive/README.md: 'Note: coding-style.md and patterns.md were part of Rules System Overhaul'
rules-system-security-review.md: 'Enforcement table references coding-style.md' (should be: code-standards.md)
CLAUDE.md Section 7: 'See coding-style.md in rules/' (stale reference)
prevention: Create pre-commit hook that validates all filenames referenced in .md files exist on filesystem
Include 'Update all cross-references' in merge checklist (not just obvious includes)
Use explicit grep search for old filename in .claude/ and docs/ when deleting files
Consider symbolic link (temporary) to redirect old filename to new location while fixing references
gotchas.extracted_from: Task #104 (path conflict fixes), where 5 broken references discovered after Task #103 merge

gotchas.gotcha: Configuration files may have header comments claiming that certain tools/validators read them, but those tools may have been archived or replaced without updating the header
gotchas.context: Config System Overhaul Pipeline #10 (Task #106) discovered command-allowlist.yaml header claiming 'command-allowlist-validator.cjs reads this' but the validator was archived in Pipeline #7
gotchas.why_it_happens: When a tool is archived, the config file header is not automatically updated. Developers may assume if the config exists and is referenced in its own header, there's a consumer. But the header itself can become stale.
gotchas.symptoms: Config file exists with header claiming a consumer reads it. Developer writes code assuming the consumer processes the config. Upon wiring audit, discovers the consumer was archived and functionality was hardcoded into a different module instead.
gotchas.example: command-allowlist.yaml header: 'Read by command-allowlist-validator.cjs to validate commands'. But command-allowlist-validator.cjs was archived in Pipeline #7, and command-allowlist.cjs (the library) hardcodes the allowlist in JavaScript instead of reading the YAML file.
gotchas.trigger: Archiving a tool that reads a config file, but not updating the config file's header comment
gotchas.solution: During wiring audits, validate the config header's claimed consumers against actual require() statements in the codebase. If a consumer is archived, either: 1) Delete the config file, 2) Rewire the config to a new consumer, or 3) Update the header to reflect reality.
gotchas.detection_pattern: Grep for the validator/consumer tool name. If zero matches or only matches in the config header itself, the consumer is likely dead.
prevention: Include config file header update in archival checklist (if archiving a tool, update all config headers that reference it)
During wiring audits, validate each config's claimed consumers exist and actually read the config
gotchas.extracted_from: Task #106 findings in learnings.md ('Phantom References' section)
